details:
ARES — Autonomous Reconnaissance and Exploration System

Read the Terrain. Compare the Route. Explore Mars Intelligently.

Project Overview

ARES (Autonomous Reconnaissance and Exploration System) is an interactive Martian terrain-intelligence and mission-planning platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, addressing the challenge Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map.

As humanity advances toward sustained exploration of Mars, understanding the Martian landscape becomes increasingly important. Every potential journey across the planet raises essential questions: What terrain lies between two destinations? How does elevation change along a route? Which geographical features could influence the journey? How can scientific data support more informed exploration decisions?

ARES brings these questions into a unified digital environment by transforming NASA-derived planetary data into interactive visualizations, computational terrain assessments, route-planning models, and scientific mission reports.

The central vision behind ARES is to make Mars exploration more analytical, accessible, and interactive by connecting planetary science with computational decision-making.

How ARES Works

Interactive Martian Exploration

ARES features an interactive three-dimensional Mars globe powered by Three.js, complemented by a detailed two-dimensional planetary map built with Leaflet.

Users can explore the Martian surface, inspect geographic coordinates, and establish starting points and destinations for simulated exploration missions. The connected mapping interfaces provide a unified geographical workspace for investigating potential routes across the planet.

NASA-Powered Terrain Intelligence

At the scientific core of ARES is elevation data derived from NASA's Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA), an instrument aboard the Mars Global Surveyor spacecraft.

The system processes digital elevation models using geospatial and numerical computing techniques to retrieve elevation measurements, estimate surface gradients, and investigate regional terrain characteristics.

ARES translates these calculations into a visual terrain-classification system featuring Low, Moderate, High, and Extreme slope categories. The resulting hazard-analysis overlays allow users to examine the relationship between topography and modeled route conditions.

NASA Mars Trek imagery provides additional visual context, connecting the analytical capabilities of ARES with recognizable Martian geography.

Intelligent Route Planning and Algorithmic Comparison

ARES implements established pathfinding algorithms, including A* search and Dijkstra's algorithm, to evaluate different route-planning objectives.

Its terrain-weighted A* model considers geographical distance alongside modeled terrain penalties, while Dijkstra's algorithm provides a distance-oriented comparison.

By examining alternative computational approaches, users can investigate how different priorities influence route selection.

ARES also incorporates broader planetary route exploration, allowing users to investigate journeys across larger geographical areas of Mars.

Route Intelligence and Scientific Analysis

Beyond displaying calculated routes, ARES provides an integrated analytical environment containing route distances, waypoints, terrain-exposure indicators, elevation profiles, and comparative pathfinding results.

The Science Lab presents geographically relevant terrain information, while the Route Scientific Report organizes calculated results into an interpretable scientific overview.

An additional Mission Decision Brief connects these findings to the selected mission, presenting a structured explanation of the calculated terrain and route characteristics.

Together, these components transform ARES from a visualization interface into an integrated platform for investigating Martian terrain and modeled exploration decisions.

Technologies and Development

ARES combines planetary data processing, computational algorithms, web technologies, and interactive scientific visualization.

Its backend is developed in Python, using Flask to provide application programming interfaces, Rasterio to process geospatial elevation datasets, and NumPy for numerical calculations.

The frontend is built using JavaScript, HTML, and CSS, with Three.js enabling three-dimensional planetary visualization and Leaflet supporting interactive two-dimensional mapping.

ARES integrates NASA MOLA-derived elevation datasets and NASA Mars Trek imagery. Its source code and technical documentation are maintained through GitHub, while the interactive application is publicly deployed using Render.

The project includes a documented scientific methodology, algorithm descriptions, numerical validation, and browser-based testing.

Creativity and Innovation

The defining innovation of ARES lies in its integration of scientific terrain analysis, planetary visualization, comparative algorithms, and interpretable mission intelligence within a single cohesive environment.

Rather than presenting isolated maps, elevation measurements, or route calculations, ARES connects these capabilities into a continuous exploration workflow.

A user can begin by examining Mars in three dimensions, select a destination, investigate surrounding terrain characteristics, generate computational routes, compare optimization objectives, and inspect the scientific reasoning behind the resulting mission information.

This integration brings together planetary science, geospatial computing, algorithmic exploration, and interactive design.

Another important feature of ARES is its emphasis on explainability. The platform presents the underlying terrain classifications, computational route characteristics, and scientific measurements alongside its visual outputs, making the analytical process accessible to users.

The result is an application designed not merely to display the Martian surface, but to encourage meaningful investigation of the geographical information behind exploration decisions.

Benefits and Intended Impact

ARES demonstrates how publicly available NASA scientific resources can be transformed into accessible tools for planetary exploration and scientific learning.

Its interactive environment offers educational value to students, researchers, astronomy enthusiasts, and individuals interested in planetary geography, robotics, computational science, and future space missions.

The platform illustrates the practical applications of geospatial analysis, graph-search algorithms, scientific computing, and data visualization in the context of an extraordinary real-world challenge: exploring another planet.

By bringing scientific measurements and computational models into a shared environment, ARES encourages evidence-based reasoning about Martian geography and exploration.

Its broader vision is to contribute toward increasingly integrated planetary exploration systems, where scientific observations, geographic information, and computational analysis work together to support informed decisions.

Project Vision

ARES was independently directed and developed as a solo project, bringing together planetary science, programming, mathematical modeling, and interactive visualization.

The project reflects a central idea: the value of planetary data grows when people can explore it, analyze it, and understand what it reveals.

Through its integrated Mars globe, NASA-derived terrain intelligence, algorithmic route planning, and scientific mission reports, ARES offers an interactive approach to investigating the challenges and possibilities of exploring Mars.

ARES — Turning Martian terrain data into exploration intelligence.
